intro: Hi, I'm the Veredicto guide. Veredicto checks an AI idea against the EU AI Act before anyone builds it. Type an idea in the box at the top and the tile turns over to its verdict. Further down, the hall shows the six people every idea passes. Ask me about the hall, the case study, or how the screening works.
how: Here is how it works. A model turns a proposal into facts, and every fact has to quote the sentence it came from. Code throws out any fact whose quote is not in the text. Then the rules for Article 5, Annex III and Article 50 run in code, so the same proposal always gets the same answer. Disputed cases go to a review queue instead of getting a confident verdict.
hall: The hall is the story of one idea. A visitor carries it past six people: the Reader, the Checker, the Law clerk, the Challenger, the Writer and the Reviewer. Each gives an opinion, and a tile turns over to show the verdict. The people are a picture of the steps. In the software some are a model, some are code, and one is a real person. Open The hall from the home page to walk your own idea through.
screen: Screen your file takes a whole file of proposals. Drop a CSV with a column called proposal, or press Use the sample file. Each proposal passes the six people and lands in the list with its verdict. Open a row to see why, and download the results when it finishes. Your file is read in your browser and goes nowhere else.
case: The case study is Cierzo Seguros, a fictional Spanish health and life insurer. Its six AI systems sit on the ladder on the inventory page, one step for each risk level. Pick a system to see why it sits there. Two are high-risk, one needs a transparency notice, two are minimal risk, and one, still being bought, includes a prohibited use: reading call-centre agents' emotions from their voice. The chatbot not saying it is an AI is the one obligation already overdue.
fairness: The fairness page starts with three questions. Guess first, then see what the data says. The health pricing model was rebuilt on official Spanish data: 14,336 adults from the national health survey, with care priced at Osakidetza's official tariffs. People born abroad would pay about 1.17 times their share of the cost. The interval reaches 1, so it is a signal to watch, not a proven breach.
obligations: The obligations page puts a date on every gap. Drag the date and each square, one per obligation, turns green, amber or red as it falls due. The emotion tool is already banned. The chatbot's AI notice has applied since August 2026. Marking AI-generated text is due in December 2026, and the two high-risk systems need to comply by December 2027.
eu: This page uses the European Commission's catalogue of AI in Europe's public sector. Every square on the wall is one real system that a public body already runs, coloured by its verdict. Point at a square to see what it is, and click to open it. The tier is a first pass for a person to confirm.
stress: The stress test takes twenty practices and phrases each one plainly and in disguise. Pick a practice to see both wordings side by side, with what the free keyword reader said. It does well on plain wording and badly on disguise. That gap is the case for a model reader, and the quote check is what keeps a model honest.
intake: This is the proposal intake. Each row is an AI idea from a business team, with a verdict, the articles behind it, and its obligations. Open one to see the sentences the reader quoted. To screen your own, open Screen your file.
documents: These are the full documents behind the case study, as folders on a shelf. Start with the one-page summary or the classification. Then come the fundamental rights impact assessment and the gap assessment, and the four decision records.
why: Why it matters now: Accenture's Future of Work Trends 2026 reports that roles needing AI governance skills roughly tripled between 2022 and 2025. Companies need a repeatable way to check AI ideas early, not a one-off legal review.
legal: No. This is a portfolio project and not legal advice. The law is real and current to 27 September 2026, but Cierzo Seguros is fictional.
who: Veredicto was built by Marco Ortiz Togashi, a Master in Business Analytics and Data Science student at IE University. The code and the data are on GitHub.
highrisk: Under the AI Act, a system is high-risk when it is a safety part of a regulated product, or when it is used in an Annex III area such as hiring, credit, insurance pricing, education, public benefits or law enforcement. High-risk systems need risk management, data governance, human oversight, logging and registration.
aiact: The EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689, sorts AI by risk. A few practices are banned outright, high-risk uses carry heavy duties, some systems only need to tell people they are AI, and the rest are left alone. The Digital Omnibus moved some of its dates.
data: The case study uses two official Spanish sources: the national health survey from INE, and the Osakidetza tariff to price care. The live page uses the European Commission's Public Sector Tech Watch catalogue, checked every morning.
runs: It runs on Azure OpenAI, Claude on Azure Foundry, or the Claude API. It also runs fully offline with a keyword reader and no key, which is what the free daily run uses.
idea: Describe the idea in a sentence or two: what the AI does, and who it affects. I'll check it against the AI Act, show which of your words decided it, and ask a follow-up when an answer could change the verdict.
supply: This page checks twelve supply-chain AI ideas against the AI Act. Pick a tile to read the idea. Forecasting, routing and inspecting things is left alone. The law bites where the AI judges people: allocating work to warehouse staff, ranking their productivity, hiring, or reading their emotions. Where a small change lowers the tier, switch it on and the tile turns over.
fallback: I can explain this page, the hall and its six people, the case study, the fairness evidence, the live EU data, how the screening works, or what high-risk means. Try one of the suggestions below.
